translationRepairs: On one occasion, he and Ji An, the Commandant of the Palace Guard, jointly sought a private audience. Ji An spoke first, and Gongsun Hong followed up with supporting arguments. The Emperor was invariably pleased and accepted everything they said. In this way, Gongsun Hong's standing grew day by day.

On one occasion, he and Ji An, the Commandant of Noble Ranks, jointly sought a private audience. Ji An spoke first, and Gongsun Hong followed up with supporting arguments. The Emperor was invariably pleased and accepted everything they said. In this way, Gongsun Hong's standing grew day by day.
主爵都尉 is the commandant who administered noble ranks, not the palace guard; the replacement restores the office without other changes.

Once, together with the Commandant of the Palace Guard Ji An, they sought a private audience. Ji An spoke first, and Hong followed up after him. The Emperor was always pleased, and everything they said was accepted. Because of this, Hong grew daily in the Emperor's favor.

Once, together with the Commandant of Noble Ranks Ji An, they sought a private audience. Ji An spoke first, and Hong followed up after him. The Emperor was always pleased, and everything they said was accepted. Because of this, Hong grew daily in the Emperor's favor.
The same office 主爵都尉 is mistranslated as Palace Guard in the literal line; Commandant of Noble Ranks is the accurate title.
The execution of Zhufu Yan and the banishment of Dong Zhongshu to Jiaxi were both the work of Gongsun Hong.
The execution of Zhufu Yan and the banishment of Dong Zhongshu to Jiaoxi were both the work of Gongsun Hong.
膠西 is the kingdom Jiaoxi; Jiaxi drops the vowel and names a different place.
The execution of Zhufu Yan and the exile of Dong Zhongshu to Jiaxi were both accomplished through Hong's efforts.
The execution of Zhufu Yan and the exile of Dong Zhongshu to Jiaoxi were both accomplished through Hong's efforts.
The literal line repeats Jiaxi for 膠西; Jiaoxi is the correct toponym.
Therefore, it is said: 'To practice with vigor is close to benevolence; to love inquiry is close to wisdom; to know shame is close to courage.
Therefore, it is said: 'To practice with vigor is close to benevolence; to love inquiry is close to wisdom; to know shame is close to courage.'
The Chinese nested quotation 故曰『…』 is a closed saying; the literal English opened the quote and never closed it.
The Imperial Censor Cheng Jin remonstrated: 'This must not be done.
The Imperial Censor Cheng remonstrated: 'This must not be done.
御史成 names the censor 成; 進諫曰 is the verb of remonstrance, so Jin is an invented given name.
The Imperial Censor Cheng Jin remonstrated and said: 'This must not be done.
The Imperial Censor Cheng remonstrated and said: 'This must not be done.
The literal line likewise treats 進諫 as a name; the speaker is Imperial Censor Cheng.

Thus, even if there were powerful states with strong armies, Your Majesty could pursue running beasts, shoot at flying birds, roam broadly through the royal park at Yan, indulge in the most extravagant spectacles, and enjoy the full thrill of riding—all without concern.

Thus, even if there were powerful states with strong armies, Your Majesty could pursue running beasts, shoot at flying birds, roam broadly through parks of excursion and banquet, indulge in the most extravagant spectacles, and enjoy the full thrill of riding—all without concern.
游燕之囿 is parks for excursion and feasting (燕 for 宴), not a royal park in the state of Yan.

Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised the banner in Chen; wuchen and Zhang Er in Zhao; Xiang Liang in Wu; Tian Dan in Qi; Jing Ju in Ying; Zhou Shi in Wei; Han Guang in Yan. From every remote mountain and hidden valley, men of ambition rose up simultaneously—too many to record.

Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised the banner in Chen; Wu Chen and Zhang Er in Zhao; Xiang Liang in Wu; Tian Dan in Qi; Jing Ju in Ying; Zhou Shi in Wei; Han Guang in Yan. From every remote mountain and hidden valley, men of ambition rose up simultaneously—too many to record.
武臣 is the personal name Wu Chen, listed with Zhang Er; lowercase wuchen is a formatting error, not a different person.

Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised Chen, wuchen and Zhang Er raised Zhao, Xiang Liang raised Wu, Tian Dan raised Qi, Jing Ju raised Ying, Zhou Shi raised Wei, and Han Guang raised Yan. Heroes from remote mountains and hidden valleys rose together—too many to record.

Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised Chen, Wu Chen and Zhang Er raised Zhao, Xiang Liang raised Wu, Tian Dan raised Qi, Jing Ju raised Ying, Zhou Shi raised Wei, and Han Guang raised Yan. Heroes from remote mountains and hidden valleys rose together—too many to record.
The literal line repeats lowercase wuchen for 武臣; Wu Chen restores the personal name.
Thus, Zhufu Yan's entire clan was executed.
Thus Zhufu Yan was executed along with his entire clan.
族主父偃 applies the clan-extermination penalty to Zhufu Yan himself together with his kin, as the surrounding confession and plea to execute him already show.

Let the next descendant of Gongsun Hong in the line of succession be granted the rank of Marquis Within the Passes, with an estate of three hundred households. He is to be summoned to the capital, his name presented to the Imperial Secretariat, and I shall personally preside over his investiture.'

Let the next descendant of Gongsun Hong in the line of succession be granted the rank of Marquis Within the Passes, with an estate of three hundred households. He is to be summoned to the imperial carriage office, his name presented to the Imperial Secretariat, and I shall personally preside over his investiture.'
徵詣公車 names the Gongju, the imperial carriage office that received summons, which 'the capital' omits; the proposed parenthetical 公车 is not natural English.

Bu Shi was tested among the shepherds, Sang Hongyang was raised from among the merchants, Wei Qing rose from servitude, and Jin Midi emerged from among captured barbarians. These were the counterparts of those ancient men who pounded walls and fed cattle.

Bu Shi was tested among the shepherds, Sang Hongyang was raised from among the merchants, Wei Qing rose from servitude, and Jin Midi emerged from among surrendered captives. These were the counterparts of those ancient men who pounded walls and fed cattle.
降虜 are surrendered captives; captured barbarians adds ethnicity and replaces surrender with capture.
The accumulated roster of illustrious ministers also followed in their wake.
The accumulated roster of illustrious ministers also ranks next after them.
亦其次也 ranks the later roster as next after the Wu-era peak, not merely as those who followed in sequence.
